title: K. Extremal Geometry Glossary
description: Combinatorial and extremal geometry terms referenced throughout the pentagonal multi-sheeted framework, connecting distance-geometric phenomena to classical problems of Erdős, Falconer, Guth–Katz, and Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter.

distance-set.summary: The set of all distinct pairwise distances among points in a finite point set P.
distance-set.definition:
Given a finite point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the **distance set** is

$$\Delta(P) = \{ \|p - q\| : p, q \in P, \; p \neq q \}.$$

Its size $|\Delta(P)|$ is the **number of distinct distances**. Erdős (1946) asked: what is the minimum of $|\Delta(P)|$ over $n$-point sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$?

For the pentagonal lattice $\mathcal{L} \subset \mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$, the norm-multiplicativity of $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ ensures that **many pairs share the same distance**, giving a distance set much smaller than the trivial $\binom{n}{2}$ upper bound.

examples.title: Integer Grid Distance Set
examples.body: For the $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ integer grid, the distance set is determined by integers expressible as sums of two squares. The rich multiplicative structure of $\mathbb{Z}$ causes many pairs to share the same distance, minimizing $|\Delta(P)|$.

examples.title: Pentagonal Lattice Distance Set
examples.body: In $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$, the norm form $N(a + b\phi) = a^2 + ab\phi - b^2\phi$ has factorization properties related to $a^2 + b^2$ but with a richer prime structure. Primes split or remain inert in $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ according to quadratic reciprocity mod 5, producing a distance set potentially smaller than the integer grid in some regimes.

formulas.expression: \Delta(P) = \{ \|p - q\| : p, q \in P, \; p \neq q \}
formulas.description: The distance set of a finite point set P, collecting all distinct pairwise Euclidean distances.

variables.\\|p - q\\|: Euclidean distance between points p and q

references: Erdős, P. (1946). On sets of distances of n points. American Mathematical Monthly, 53(5), 248–250.

distance-ring.summary: The set of all lattice points at a fixed distance r from a reference point, whose multiplicity is the engine of distance-coincidence counts.
distance-ring.definition:
The set of points at a fixed distance $r$ from a reference point $p_0$:

$$R_r(p_0) = \{ q \in \mathcal{L} : \|q - p_0\| = r \}.$$

In the pentagonal lattice, $|R_r|$ can be very large — a consequence of the many ways a $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ element can factor while preserving norm. Distance rings of high multiplicity are the **engine of high distance-coincidence counts**.

examples.title: High-Multiplicity Distance Ring
examples.body: In $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$, a norm value $r^2$ may be achieved by many distinct elements $a + b\phi$ with different $(a, b)$ pairs, each corresponding to a distinct lattice point on the distance ring $R_r(p_0)$. This multiplicity grows with the number of factorizations of $r^2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$.

formulas.description: The distance ring of radius r centered at reference point p_0 within lattice L.

distance-web.summary: The graph with vertex set equal to a lattice and edges between every pair of points at exactly distance r, exhibiting unusually dense local structure in pentagonal lattices.
distance-web.definition: The graph $W_r$ with vertex set $\mathcal{L}$ and an edge between every pair at distance exactly $r$. The pentagonal distance webs have unusually dense local structure due to the **norm-multiplicativity degeneracy**.

examples.title: Pentagonal Distance Web Density
examples.body: For a common distance $r$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$, the graph $W_r$ has high average degree because many lattice points lie on each distance ring. The local neighborhoods in $W_r$ reflect the 5- or 10-fold rotational symmetry of the pentagonal lattice.

equidistant-family.summary: A set of points with all pairwise distances equal, forming a regular simplex; extremal configurations for the unit-distance problem.
equidistant-family.definition:
A set of points with all pairwise distances equal — i.e., a regular simplex. In 2D, the maximum size is 3 (equilateral triangle); in 3D, 4 (regular tetrahedron).

Equidistant families are extremal configurations for the unit-distance problem.

examples.title: Equilateral Triangle in 2D
examples.body: Three points forming an equilateral triangle constitute the largest equidistant family in $\mathbb{R}^2$. All three pairwise distances are equal, making this a degenerate case of the unit-distance problem.

examples.title: Regular Tetrahedron in 3D
examples.body: Four points forming a regular tetrahedron constitute the largest equidistant family in $\mathbb{R}^3$. All six pairwise distances are equal.

erdos-distinct-distances.summary: The problem of determining the minimum number of distinct distances among n points in the plane, conjectured by Erdős to be Ω(n/√log n).
erdos-distinct-distances.definition:
Let $g(n) = \min_{|P| = n} |\Delta(P)|$. Erdős (1946) conjectured

$$g(n) = \Omega\!\left( \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}} \right),$$

achieved (he showed) by the $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ integer grid.

The integer grid $\{1, \dots, \sqrt{n}\}^2$ minimizes $|\Delta(P)|$ via the rich multiplicative structure of $\mathbb{Z}$ (sums of two squares, divisor functions). The pentagonal lattice $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$ has **even richer multiplicative structure**, raising the question of whether it matches or beats the integer grid in some regimes.

examples.title: Integer Grid Achieves the Bound
examples.body: The $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ integer grid has $|\Delta(P)| = O(n / \sqrt{\log n})$ because many pairs of integers $(a, b)$ satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = k$ for the same small integer $k$, collapsing many distances into one.

examples.title: Pentagonal Lattice Question
examples.body: The norm form $N(a + b\phi) = a^2 + ab\phi - b^2\phi$ has factorization properties related to $a^2 + b^2$ but with a richer prime structure — primes split or remain inert in $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ according to quadratic reciprocity mod 5. This raises the open question: does $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$ match or beat the Erdős bound?

formulas.description: Erdős's conjectured lower bound on the minimum number of distinct distances among n points in the plane.

variables.g(n): Minimum number of distinct distances over all n-point sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$

references: Erdős, P. (1946). On sets of distances of n points. American Mathematical Monthly, 53(5), 248–250.
Guth, L., & Katz, N. H. (2015). On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane. Annals of Mathematics, 181(1), 155–190.

guth-katz-theorem.summary: The landmark 2010 result proving g(n) = Ω(n/log n), nearly resolving the Erdős distinct distances conjecture using polynomial partitioning and incidence geometry.
guth-katz-theorem.definition:
Larry Guth and Nets Katz proved

$$g(n) = \Omega\!\left( \frac{n}{\log n} \right),$$

nearly matching the conjectured bound. Their proof combined:

- **Polynomial partitioning** (a new technique).
- **Incidence geometry** of lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
- **Algebraic methods** (the Cayley–Salmon theorem on ruled surfaces).

The Guth–Katz theorem is one of the great triumphs of modern combinatorial geometry.

examples.title: Polynomial Partitioning
examples.body: Guth and Katz introduced the technique of partitioning the plane using a low-degree polynomial whose zero set divides the point set into roughly equal parts. This allowed them to apply divide-and-conquer arguments with algebraic control over the geometry.

examples.title: Reduction to Line Incidences in R³
examples.body: The proof lifts the 2D distinct distances problem to a 3D line incidence problem via the Elekes–Sharir framework, then applies the Cayley–Salmon theorem on ruled quadric surfaces to bound the incidences.

formulas.description: The Guth–Katz lower bound on the minimum number of distinct distances among n points in the plane.

variables.g(n): Minimum number of distinct distances over all n-point sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$

references: Guth, L., & Katz, N. H. (2015). On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane. Annals of Mathematics, 181(1), 155–190.
Cayley–Salmon theorem on ruled surfaces.

unit-distance-problem.summary: The problem of determining the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in the plane, bounded above by O(n^{4/3}) and below by Ω(n^{1+c/log log n}).
unit-distance-problem.definition:
Let $u(n)$ be the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Erdős (1946) asked: what is $u(n)$?

The **Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter bound** gives $u(n) = O(n^{4/3})$, proven via the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem on point–line incidences. The bound is conjectured to be far from tight; the true growth is suspected to be $n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$ or similar.

In the pentagonal lattice, unit-distance multiplicity is governed by **units of $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$** (powers of $\phi$). Unit distances in the lattice correspond to Pell-like solutions, and the resulting unit-distance graphs have a distinctive "pinwheel" structure.

examples.title: Integer Grid Lower Bound
examples.body: Erdős showed $u(n) = \Omega(n^{1 + c / \log\log n})$ via the integer grid — many integer pairs $(a, b)$ have $a^2 + b^2$ equal to small integers, producing many unit distances after appropriate scaling.

examples.title: Pentagonal Pinwheel Unit Distances
examples.body: In $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$, unit distances correspond to elements of norm 1 in $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$, i.e., solutions to the Pell-like equation $a^2 + ab\phi - b^2\phi = 1$. The units of $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ are powers of $\phi$, generating a pinwheel pattern of unit-distance directions.

formulas.description: Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter upper bound on the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in the plane.

variables.u(n): Maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in $\mathbb{R}^2$

formulas.description: Erdős lower bound on the maximum number of unit-distance pairs, achieved by the integer grid.

references: Erdős, P. (1946). On sets of distances of n points. American Mathematical Monthly, 53(5), 248–250.
Spencer, J., Szemerédi, E., & Trotter, W. T. (1984). Unit distances in the Euclidean plane. Graph Theory and Combinatorics, 294–304.

spencer-szemeredi-trotter-bound.summary: The O(n^{4/3}) upper bound on the number of unit-distance pairs among n points in the plane, derived from the Szemerédi–Trotter incidence theorem.
spencer-szemeredi-trotter-bound.definition:
The bound $u(n) = O(n^{4/3})$ on the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Proven via the **Szemerédi–Trotter theorem** on point–line incidences (and its generalizations to circles). The bound is conjectured to be far from tight; the true growth is suspected to be $n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$ or similar.

examples.title: Circle Incidence Reduction
examples.body: Unit distances between n points correspond to incidences between n points and n unit circles (one centered at each point). The Szemerédi–Trotter theorem, generalized to circles, bounds these incidences by $O(n^{4/3})$.

formulas.description: Upper bound on the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in the plane.

variables.u(n): Maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in $\mathbb{R}^2$

references: Spencer, J., Szemerédi, E., & Trotter, W. T. (1984). Unit distances in the Euclidean plane. Graph Theory and Combinatorics, 294–304.
Szemerédi, E., & Trotter, W. T. (1983). Extremal problems in discrete geometry. Combinatorica, 3(3–4), 381–392.

pinwheel-polygon.summary: A polygon engineered so that a chosen subset of edges reconnects into a target lattice, with the canonical example being the Conway–Radin pinwheel triangle that tiles the plane aperiodically with infinitely many distinct orientations.
pinwheel-polygon.definition:
A polygon engineered such that a **chosen subset of edges** (the active set $E_A$) reconnects into a target lattice — typically $\mathbb{Z}^2$ — while the other edges are decorative.

The canonical example is the **Conway–Radin pinwheel triangle**: a right triangle with legs in ratio $1:2$, which tiles $\mathbb{R}^2$ aperiodically with infinitely many distinct tile orientations (a "statistically rotationally invariant" tiling).

examples.title: Conway–Radin Pinwheel Triangle
examples.body: A right triangle with legs of length 1 and 2 (hypotenuse $\sqrt{5}$). Five copies tile a scaled version of the same triangle, and iterating this substitution produces an aperiodic tiling of the plane in which tiles appear in infinitely many distinct orientations, densifying $S^1$.

references: Radin, C. (1994). The pinwheel tilings of the plane. Annals of Mathematics, 139(3), 661–702.
Conway, J. H., & Radin, C. (1998). Quaquaversal tilings and rotations. Inventiones Mathematicae, 132(1), 179–188.

pinwheel-phenomenon.summary: The density of (distance, direction) pairs in pentagonal lattices, where many point pairs share the same distance but have different directions that densify the unit circle.
pinwheel-phenomenon.definition:
The **density of (distance, direction) pairs** in pentagonal lattices: many pairs of points are at the same distance but in different directions, with the directions densifying $S^1$.

This is closely connected to:

- **Distance-direction problem** (Erdős–Purdy).
- **Equidistribution** of pentagonal lattice points on circles.
- **Quasicrystal diffraction**, where pinwheel-like density appears in Fourier space.

### Why Pentagonal Lattices Pinwheel

The orientation group $\Gamma = \mathbb{Z}_{10}$ (or its rotational subgroup $\mathbb{Z}_5$) generates 10 (or 5) distinct directions per distance ring. Combined with the rich norm-multiplicativity, the lattice exhibits **explosive direction multiplicity** at common distances.

examples.title: 10-fold Direction Multiplicity
examples.body: For a common distance $r$ in the pentagonal lattice, the orientation group $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ generates 10 distinct directions in which point pairs at distance $r$ can be oriented. As $r$ ranges over all distances, these directions densify $S^1$.

examples.title: Quasicrystal Diffraction Analogy
examples.body: In quasicrystal diffraction patterns, the Fourier transform of the point set exhibits 5- or 10-fold symmetry with sharp peaks. The pinwheel phenomenon in the pentagonal lattice is the real-space counterpart of this Fourier-space structure.

references: Radin, C. (1994). The pinwheel tilings of the plane. Annals of Mathematics, 139(3), 661–702.
Erdős, P., & Purdy, G. (1971). Some extremal problems in combinatorial geometry.

degeneracy-engine.summary: The algebraic mechanism by which norm-multiplicativity of Z[φ] produces many distance coincidences: unique factorization in Z[φ] means many distinct factorizations yield the same norm value.
degeneracy-engine.definition:
The mechanism producing many distance coincidences: $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ is a UFD, so norms factor uniquely, and many distinct factorizations give the same norm value. Each factorization is a distinct (point, point) pair at the corresponding distance.

The **degeneracy engine** is the algebraic source of all distance-geometric phenomena in the pentagonal framework. The **pinwheel phenomenon** is its geometric manifestation: a dense, multi-directional, distance-coincident point pattern with no Euclidean analogue.

examples.title: Multiple Factorizations, Same Norm
examples.body: In $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$, a norm value $N = r^2$ may factor as $N = \pi_1 \bar{\pi}_1 = \pi_2 \bar{\pi}_2 = \cdots$ in multiple ways (where $\pi_i$ are Gaussian-like primes in $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$). Each factorization corresponds to a distinct element $a + b\phi$ with $N(a + b\phi) = N$, hence a distinct lattice point at distance $r$ from the origin.

formulas.description: The norm form of Z[φ], whose multiplicativity is the algebraic source of distance coincidences in the pentagonal lattice.

falconer-distance-problem.summary: The conjecture that a compact set E ⊂ ℝⁿ with Hausdorff dimension greater than n/2 has a distance set of positive Lebesgue measure; the continuous analogue of the Erdős distinct distances problem.
falconer-distance-problem.definition:
For a compact set $E \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the Falconer distance problem asks:

> If $\dim_H(E) > s_n$ for some threshold $s_n$, does $\Delta(E)$ have positive Lebesgue measure?

Falconer (1985) conjectured $s_n = n/2$. The conjecture remains open in all dimensions $n \geq 2$.

**Continuous Analogue of Erdős**: Erdős asks for finite point sets; Falconer asks for fractal sets. The interplay is deep:

- **Erdős**: discrete combinatorial bounds.
- **Falconer**: measure-theoretic / harmonic analysis bounds.

Both ultimately concern how rich the distance structure of a set can be.

**Pentagonal Connection**: The pentagonal multi-sheeted tilings have fractal-like dimensional behavior under BFS volume growth (effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}$ can be non-integer near vortices). Falconer-type questions about their distance sets are natural — and largely unexplored.

examples.title: Threshold Dimension n/2
examples.body: Falconer showed that for almost all rigid motions of a compact set $E$ with $\dim_H(E) > n/2$, the distance set $\Delta(E)$ has positive Lebesgue measure. The conjecture is that the 'almost all' qualifier can be removed.

examples.title: Pentagonal Fractal Dimension
examples.body: Near vortex defects in the pentagonal multi-sheeted tiling, the BFS volume growth $V(r) \sim r^{d_{\text{eff}}}$ yields a non-integer effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}$. This fractal-like behavior makes Falconer-type distance questions natural for these structures.

formulas.description: Falconer's conjecture: Hausdorff dimension exceeding n/2 implies the distance set has positive Lebesgue measure.

variables.\\dim_H(E): Hausdorff dimension of the compact set E
variables.|\\Delta(E)|: Lebesgue measure of the distance set

references: Falconer, K. J. (1985). On the Hausdorff dimensions of distance sets. Mathematika, 32(2), 206–212.

incidence-geometry.summary: The study of incidences between geometric objects such as points and lines, foundational to unit-distance bounds and Erdős-type results.
incidence-geometry.definition:
The study of incidences between geometric objects — primarily points and lines (or curves) — and the combinatorial bounds on how many incidences can occur.

Generalizations include:
- **Points and circles**: incidence bounds with extra logarithmic factors.
- **Points and curves**: depending on the curve family's "degree of freedom".
- **Higher dimensions**: Guth, Solymosi, and others.

These bounds underlie unit-distance bounds and Erdős-type results.

examples.title: Point-Line Incidences
examples.body: Given $n$ points and $m$ lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem bounds the number of incidences (point-line pairs where the point lies on the line) by $O((nm)^{2/3} + n + m)$.

examples.title: Application to Unit Distances
examples.body: Unit distances between $n$ points correspond to incidences between $n$ points and $n$ unit circles. Generalizing Szemerédi–Trotter to circles yields the Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter bound $u(n) = O(n^{4/3})$.

references: Szemerédi, E., & Trotter, W. T. (1983). Extremal problems in discrete geometry. Combinatorica, 3(3–4), 381–392.

szemeredi-trotter-theorem.summary: The foundational theorem of incidence geometry bounding the number of point-line incidences by O((nm)^{2/3} + n + m), tight up to constants.
szemeredi-trotter-theorem.definition:
For $n$ points and $m$ lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the number of incidences is

$$I(P, L) = O\!\left( (nm)^{2/3} + n + m \right).$$

This is the foundational theorem of incidence geometry. Tight up to constants.

examples.title: Tightness of the Bound
examples.body: The Szemerédi–Trotter bound is achieved (up to constants) by a construction using a $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ grid of points and lines through many grid points. This shows the exponent $2/3$ cannot be improved.

formulas.description: Upper bound on the number of point-line incidences for n points and m lines in the plane.

variables.I(P, L): Number of incidences (point-line pairs where the point lies on the line)

references: Szemerédi, E., & Trotter, W. T. (1983). Extremal problems in discrete geometry. Combinatorica, 3(3–4), 381–392.

polynomial-method.summary: A technique using low-degree polynomials vanishing on point sets to extract incidence bounds, pioneered by Dvir and Guth and central to the Guth–Katz theorem.
polynomial-method.definition:
Pioneered by Dvir (finite field Kakeya) and Guth (joints theorem), the polynomial method uses **low-degree polynomials vanishing on point sets** to extract incidence bounds. It revolutionized combinatorial geometry in the 2000s–2010s.

Key applications:
- **Dvir's finite field Kakeya theorem**: a polynomial of degree $< n$ vanishing on $n$ points in each direction must vanish everywhere.
- **Guth's joints theorem**: bounding the number of joints (points where 3 non-coplanar lines meet) using polynomial vanishing.
- **Guth–Katz theorem**: polynomial partitioning as a divide-and-conquer tool for distinct distances.

examples.title: Dvir's Finite Field Kakeya
examples.body: Dvir (2009) proved that a Kakeya set in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ (containing a line in every direction) has size $\Omega(q^n)$. The proof: a polynomial of degree $< q$ vanishing on the set would vanish on all of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ by the Schwartz–Zippel lemma, contradiction.

examples.title: Polynomial Partitioning in Guth–Katz
examples.body: Guth and Katz partition $\mathbb{R}^3$ using a polynomial $p$ of degree $D$ whose zero set $Z(p)$ divides space into $O(D^3)$ cells, each containing $O(n/D^3)$ points. This allows a divide-and-conquer argument with algebraic control.

references: Dvir, Z. (2009). On the size of Kakeya sets in finite fields. Journal of the American Mathematical Society, 22(4), 1093–1097.
Guth, L. (2010). The endpoint case of the Bennett–Carbery–Tao multilinear Kakeya conjecture. Acta Mathematica, 205(2), 263–286.
Guth, L., & Katz, N. H. (2015). On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane. Annals of Mathematics, 181(1), 155–190.

delone-set.summary: A point set that is both uniformly discrete and relatively dense, serving as the standard model for aperiodic point patterns including lattices, quasicrystals, and Penrose tiling vertices.
delone-set.definition:
A set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that is:

- **Uniformly discrete**: $\exists r > 0$ such that no two points are within $r$.
- **Relatively dense**: $\exists R > 0$ such that every $R$-ball contains a point.

Delone sets are the standard model for aperiodic point patterns — they include lattices, quasicrystal point sets, and Penrose tiling vertices.

**Pentagonal Multi-Sheeted Vertex Set**: The projection of the multi-sheeted vertex set to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a Delone set with characteristic pentagonal long-range order and characteristic vortex defects. It would in principle yield a **diffraction pattern** with 5- or 10-fold symmetry, modulated by the sheet structure.

examples.title: Integer Lattice as Delone Set
examples.body: The integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is a Delone set with $r = 1$ (minimum distance) and $R = \sqrt{2}$ (maximum gap). It is periodic, hence the simplest case.

examples.title: Penrose Tiling Vertices
examples.body: The vertex set of a Penrose tiling is a Delone set that is aperiodic (no translational symmetry) but has long-range 5-fold rotational order, visible in its diffraction pattern.

examples.title: Pentagonal Multi-Sheeted Projection
examples.body: The projection of the pentagonal multi-sheeted vertex set to $\mathbb{R}^2$ forms a Delone set with 5- or 10-fold symmetry and vortex defects, expected to produce a diffraction pattern with corresponding symmetry.

references: Moody, R. V. (1997). Meyer sets and their duals. The Mathematics of Long-Range Aperiodic Order, 403–441.
Lagarias, J. C. (1999). Geometric models for quasicrystals I. Delone sets of finite type. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 21(2), 161–191.

patch-equivalence.summary: The equivalence relation on Delone sets where two sets are locally indistinguishable if every finite patch of one appears in the other with the same frequency.
patch-equivalence.definition: Two Delone sets are **locally indistinguishable** if every finite patch of one appears in the other with the same frequency. This is the right equivalence relation for quasicrystals and aperiodic tilings.

examples.title: Penrose Tiling Local Indistinguishability
examples.body: Any two Penrose tilings (with the same inflation rules) are locally indistinguishable: every finite patch appearing in one appears in every other Penrose tiling with the same frequency. This is a hallmark of aperiodic order.

references: Moody, R. V. (1997). Meyer sets and their duals. The Mathematics of Long-Range Aperiodic Order, 403–441.

synonyms.label: local isomorphism class of a Delone set

adjacency-oracle.summary: A subroutine that returns the neighbors of a tile or vertex in the expansion family using exact arithmetic over Z[φ] to avoid floating-point ambiguity in distance comparisons.
adjacency-oracle.definition: A subroutine that, given a tile (or vertex), returns its neighbors in the expansion family — using **exact arithmetic over $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$** to avoid floating-point ambiguity in distance comparisons.

examples.title: Exact Arithmetic in Z[φ]
examples.body: Elements of $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]$ are represented as pairs $(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with value $a + b\phi$. Arithmetic operations (addition, multiplication, norm computation) are performed exactly using integer arithmetic, avoiding the rounding errors that would corrupt distance comparisons in floating-point.

bfs-breadth-first-search.summary: Standard graph traversal by increasing distance from a seed vertex, used to estimate effective dimension from volume scaling, detect closure of expansion families, and build adjacency matrices.
bfs-breadth-first-search.definition:
Standard graph traversal by increasing distance from a seed vertex. Used to:

- Estimate **effective dimension** $d_{\text{eff}}$ from volume scaling $V(r) \sim r^{d_{\text{eff}}}$.
- Detect closure of expansion families.
- Build sparse adjacency matrices for spectral analysis.

examples.title: Effective Dimension Estimation
examples.body: Running BFS from a seed vertex in the pentagonal lattice and counting $V(r)$ = number of vertices within graph distance $r$ allows estimation of the effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}$ via the scaling $V(r) \sim r^{d_{\text{eff}}}$. Near vortex defects, $d_{\text{eff}}$ may be non-integer.

examples.title: Expansion Family Closure Detection
examples.body: BFS can detect when an expansion family closes (returns to a previously visited configuration), signaling a periodic or quasi-periodic structure in the tiling.

formulas.description: Volume growth law used to estimate the effective dimension of the pentagonal lattice via BFS.

variables.V(r): Number of vertices within graph distance r from the seed

extremal-configuration.summary: A point set achieving an extreme value of a combinatorial quantity, such as minimum distinct distances or maximum unit distances; pentagonal lattices are conjectured to be near-extremal for several classical problems.
extremal-configuration.definition: A point set achieving extreme value of a combinatorial quantity — e.g., minimum $|\Delta(P)|$, maximum unit distances. Pentagonal lattices are conjectured (but not proven) to be near-extremal for several classical problems.

examples.title: Integer Grid as Extremal Configuration
examples.body: The $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ integer grid is the known extremal configuration for the Erdős distinct distances problem, achieving $|\Delta(P)| = O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.

examples.title: Pentagonal Lattice as Conjectural Near-Extremal
examples.body: The pentagonal lattice $\mathbb{Z}[\phi]^2$ is conjectured to be near-extremal for the distinct distances problem due to its richer norm-multiplicativity structure, but this has not been proven.
